items.title: Newly Pending Listings Fell 17% In October, The Biggest Year Over Year Drop Since 2023 (Zillow October Market Report)
items.description: Newly Pending Listings Fell 17% In October, The Biggest Year Over Year Drop Since 2023 (Zillow October Market Report) Completed existing home sales fell 9% annually, according to Zillow’s preliminary sales nowcast. Written by Mischa Fisher on November 5, 2026 Key findings: Zillow’s preliminary measure of existing home sales fell 8.7% year over year in October. Newly pending listings — a leading indicator of next month’s closed sales — fell 16.8% year over year, the biggest decrease since August 2023. The typical mortgage payment in October was 12.8% higher than a year ago, according to Zillow’s estimates. The Zillow Observed Rent Index rose 2.9% year over year in October as the rental market continues to strengthen. The acute sting of suddenly higher mortgage rates is having the unfortunate effect on the housing market that last month’s pending sales data foretold. As mortgage rates entrenched themselves above 7%, home sales slowed sharply in October. Existing home sales fell 8.7% year over year, though that largely reflects sales agreed to in September, when mortgage rates were below 7% for much of the month. Newly pending listings, a leading indicator for the next month’s closed sales, fell 16.8% from last October, marking the biggest annual dip since August 2023 and slowest October since 2018. November is shaping up to have an even larger contraction in sales activity, but the silver lining is that next month is likely going to be the worst of it. The pace of the slowdown is expected to ease into the new year. A jump in housing costs likely drove the slowdown. The monthly mortgage payment on the typical U.S. home was an estimated $2,004 in October, assuming a 20% down payment and excluding taxes and insurance. That’s up 12.8% from last year and 4.8% higher than in September, the biggest one-month jump in four years. For a buyer putting only 5% down and securing an FHA loan, which comes with a lower mortgage rate, the year-over-year rise has been similar at 11.8%. Once insurance, taxes and maintenance are factored in, a median-income household would spend 41.5% of its income on that monthly payment, up from 39.2% a year ago. The rise in mortgage costs is almost exclusively due to higher mortgage rates. The typical U.S. home value fell 0.6% month over month and is just 0.7% higher than a year earlier, as measured by the Zillow Home Value Index. Meanwhile, mortgage rates averaged 7.33% in October, according to Freddie Mac , up from 6.86% in September. As for-sale activity wanes, the rental market continues to strengthen. The typical U.S. rent is up 2.9% year over year, according to the Zillow Observed Rent Index. That’s the strongest annual gain in the past 19 months, and marks the seventh consecutive month that annual rent growth has increased. While there is no avoiding that this has been a very soft fall for for-sale activity, there are deals to be had for buyers able to brave the affordability headwinds in the coming months. Buyers usually have leverage this time of year when sellers try to make a deal before the holidays, and especially so this year given current market conditions. The continued inventory buildup means there is a lot of upside for sales into next year if we get rate relief. More data, including dashboards with local market data , can be found on the refreshed Zillow Research website . The Zillow November Market Report is expected to be released December 4 . Home Values & Mortgage Payments The typical U.S. home value is $364,812, according to the Zillow Home Value Index (ZHVI). ZHVI fell 0.6% month over month in October. Home values are 0.7% higher than a year earlier. The monthly mortgage payment on a typical U.S. home is $2,004, assuming a 20% down payment and excluding taxes and insurance. That is 12.8% higher than last year. Inventory There were 1.4 million homes for sale nationwide in October. Active inventory was 3.4% higher than a year earlier. Inventory rose 0.4% from September. New for-sale listings totaled 328,328 in October, down 4.2% from a year earlier and down 4.4% from September. Sales 304,105 homes were sold in October, according to the preliminary Zillow sales count nowcast. That is 8.7% lower than a year earlier and down 5.4% from September. These figures will be revised mid-month. Newly pending listings, which measures listings that changed from for-sale to pending status rather than closed sales, shows a 16.8% decrease from a year earlier and a 9.1% decrease over September. Affordability A household earning the median income would need to spend 34.7% of its income on the typical monthly mortgage payment (assuming a typically valued home and a 20% down payment, and including estimates for taxes, maintenance and insurance). That is up from 32.7% a year earlier and up from 33.5% in September. A household earning the median income would need to spend 26% of its income on the typical rent in October. That is unchanged from a year earlier and from September. Competition Homes took a median of 31 days to go pending in October. That was two days longer than a year earlier and two days longer than September. The share of listings with a price cut in October was 26.5%. That was down from 26.9% a year earlier and down from 27.3% in September. 25.6% of homes sold above list price in September, the most recent data available. That’s compared to 25.2% a year earlier and 27.5% in August. Rents The typical rent nationwide is $1,913, according to the Zillow Observed Rent Index. That’s 2.9% higher than a year earlier and flat from September. 40.4% of rental listings on Zillow offered a concession in October. That’s up from 38.7% a year earlier and up from 39.6% in September. items.title: MORE HOUSTON HOUSEHOLDS ABLE TO AFFORD A HOME AS PRICES EASE
items.description: MORE HOUSTON HOUSEHOLDS ABLE TO AFFORD A HOME AS PRICES EASE 42% of Houston-area households were able to buy a home in the third quarter HOUSTON -- (November 5, 2026) -- More Houston-area households were able to buy a home in the third quarter as home prices eased, according to the latest Housing and Rental Affordability Report from the Houston Association of Realtors. HAR's Housing Affordability Index shows that 42% of households in the Greater Houston area could afford a median-priced home, up from 39% in the third quarter of 2025. The median home price declined 0.4% year over year to $340,300 from $341,600 the prior year. The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate was 6.68%, compared with 6.57% during the same quarter last year. The typical monthly mortgage payment, including principal, taxes and insurance, was $2,520, compared with $2,510 in Q3 2025. Households needed a minimum annual income of $100,800 to purchase the median-priced home, which is flat from a year earlier. "Affordability is moving in the right direction, and that's encouraging, but we also know many consumers are still concerned about the cost of buying a home, particularly with mortgage rates remaining elevated," said HAR Chair Theresa Hill with Compass RE Texas, LLC -- Houston. "For buyers who may have been sitting on the sidelines, it's worth taking another look at what's possible. A Realtor can help buyers understand their options and determine what's realistic for their budget." Across Texas, 45% of households could afford a median-priced home in the third quarter, compared with 42% last year. The statewide median home price declined to $335,000 from $337,500, while the minimum annual income needed to purchase the median-priced home held at $92,400. Nationally, 38% of households could afford a median-priced home, up from 35% in 2025. According to the National Association of Realtors, the U.S. median home price increased to $432,900 from $426,800. The minimum qualifying income rose to $112,000 from $109,200. The chart below shows how the minimum annual household income needed to purchase a home has changed year-over-year. Rental Affordability Update Forty-four percent of Houston-area households could afford the median monthly lease payment in the third quarter of 2026, according to HAR's Rental Affordability Index. That is down from 45% in 2025. The median monthly lease was $2,195 compared with $2,200 a year earlier. A household needed a minimum annual income of $87,800 to qualify for the median lease payment, compared with $88,000 the prior year. The chart below shows how the median lease price for a single-family home has changed year-over-year. Highlights of the Q3 2026 Housing & Rental Affordability Report: • 42% of Greater Houston households could afford a median-priced home, up from 39% in Q3 2025. • The median home price declined 0.4% to $340,300 from $341,600 in Q3 2025. • The monthly mortgage payment was $2,520, compared with $2,510 in Q3 2025. • The minimum annual income needed to purchase a median-priced home was $100,800, compared with $100,400 in Q3 2025. • 44% of Houston-area households could afford the average lease payment on a single-family rental home, compared to 45% a year earlier. • The median lease price in the Houston area decreased slightly to $2,195. items.title: Mortgage Rates Fall for a Third Straight Week
items.description: Mortgage Rates Fall for a Third Straight Week By Hannah Jones Nov 05, 2026 What happened to mortgage rates this week? The Freddie Mac 30-year fixed mortgage rate fell 6 basis points to 7.18% this week as bond yields eased. That marks a third straight week of declines, though rates remain about one percentage point above year-ago levels. Markets were focused on the midterm elections and incoming jobs data, both of which shape expectations for future policy. Tuesday’s Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey came in stronger than expected, with layoffs down slightly and a significant gain in job openings. That points to a potentially strong jobs report on Friday. While solid hiring supports housing demand over time, a stronger-than-expected report could also lift bond yields and slow the pace of rate declines in the near term. Tuesday’s midterm elections gave Democrats a majority in both the House and Senate, as winning candidates connected with voters’ dissatisfaction with the economy. It is not yet clear whether the shift will be felt in the housing market. Many newly elected representatives have voiced discontent with the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, which has contributed to rising inflation, so any progress toward resolution could mean lower inflation and softer mortgage rates ahead. What does this mean for the housing market? Although rates have eased over the last few weeks, they remain above 7%, keeping many buyers on the sidelines. October marked another month of a slowing housing market , with both buyers and sellers pulling back. Pending sales fell 10.5% year over year, the steepest decline in three years, as buyers contend with diminished purchasing power. New listings fell 7.5% year over year as sellers held back, discouraged by weak demand. Still, sellers aren’t delisting in droves, which suggests they are disengaging rather than acting out of distress. With 43% of active listings having had a price reduction, buyers who can afford to participate are in a relatively strong position, facing less competition and more price cuts.

items.title: Weekly Housing Trends: U.S. Market Update (Week Ending Oct. 31, 2026)
items.description: Weekly Housing Trends: U.S. Market Update (Week Ending Oct. 31, 2026) By Joel Berner Nov 05, 2026 Welcome to this weekly housing trends update, where we bring you the latest snapshot of inventory trends, listing activity, and buyer-seller dynamics across the U.S. housing market. In addition to our monthly housing trends reports , which offer deeper insights into long-term patterns, we publish these weekly updates to provide more timely views into market changes. This effort began in response to rapid shifts in the economy and housing landscape. You can count on a new Weekly Housing Trends update, fresh weekly data each Thursday, and a weekly video from our economists to help you stay informed. What this week’s data shows Mortgage rates above 7% have once again been a major drag on the housing market this week. Buyers are seeing their purchasing power diminish, and many are simply opting out of buying homes altogether. Many sellers are opting out as well, with the knowledge that finding a buyer who will offer a desirable price is getting harder and harder. We’re seeing prices falling, fewer sellers listing, and homes spending longer on the market as the market seems to be entering its winter freeze early. For buyers who can manage to avoid financing their home purchase with a mortgage, though, opportunities for great deals abound. Our October data show the inventory of homes for sale at its closest level to pre-pandemic norms yet, and price reductions are even higher than they were last year at this time. The best time to buy a home has passed at the national level, but several markets still have their prime opportunities upcoming. Active inventory climbed 8.8% year-over-year The number of homes for sale rose 8.8% compared to a year ago, the highest weekly growth rate since late January. Inventory has been building momentum throughout the fall, rising from roughly 4% year-over-year growth in late August to nearly 9% now. The pickup is not being driven by a flood of new sellers. Instead, the slowdown in buyer activity is allowing unsold listings to accumulate, pushing the overall count higher. Year-to-date, active inventory i s up 4.9%. Homes spent 1 day longer on the market compared to a year ago Median days on market came in at 65 days, with homes selling one day slower than the same time last year. This marks the second week in a row that time on market has slowed after a long stretch reaching back to May of homes selling faster than last year. As mortgage rates top 7%, more buyers are retreating to the sidelines, and the shift could be an early signal of market slowdown. Year-to-date, time on market remains 2 days behind last year’s pace. New listings, a measure of sellers putting homes up for sale, fell 5.2% year-over-year New listing activity took a sharp turn downward this week, dropping 5.2% year over year. Sellers are discouraged because buyers are discouraged. The prices the market will bear are less appealing to sellers than they were when mortgage rates were lower, and the difference between current rates and the rates many would-be sellers are sitting on in their has grown, making relocating a less attractive proposition. The stronger new listing activity earlier in the year has the year-to-date change at -0.4%. The median listing price fell 2.1% year-over-year The median listing price dropped to $410,000, down 2.1% from the same week last year. Listing prices have now been negative on a year-over-year basis for 42 consecutive weeks. The median price per square foot also declined, falling 1.4% year over year. Mortgage rates have buyers in an affordability crunch that has diminished their willingness to pay, and the median price in the market is slowly responding. Year-to-date, median listing prices sit 1.9% below 2025 levels.

items.title: Opportunity Zone Home Price Growth Largely Tracks Other Areas
items.description: Opportunity Zone Home Price Growth Largely Tracks Other Areas by ATTOM Team | Nov 5, 2026 | Home Sales & Prices , Real Estate News - Recent Articles Median home prices grew year-over-year in 48.9 percent of Opportunity Zone census tracts, compared to 51.6 percent of tracts outside the zones. IRVINE, Cal. — Nov. 5, 2026 — ATTOM , the leading provider of property data , AI-powered intelligence , and real estate analytics solutions, today released its third-quarter 2026 report analyzing qualified low-income Opportunity Zones targeted by Congress for economic redevelopment in the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 (see full methodology below). In this report, ATTOM looked at 3,805 census tracts in Opportunity Zones around the United States with sufficient data to analyze, meaning they had at least five home sales in the third quarter of the year. Median single-family home and condo prices rose quarter-over-quarter in 48.1 percent (1,651) of the 3,431 Opportunity Zone tracts with sufficient data in both the second and third quarter. Year-over-year, home prices rose in 48.9 percent (1,598) of the 3,265 tracts with sufficient data in the third quarters of 2025 and 2026. Typical home prices rose year-over-year in 51.6 percent (28,212) of the 54,704 census tracts outside of Opportunity Zones with sufficient data in both quarters to be included in the analysis, meaning that price growth was more common outside the targeted economic development zones than inside them. In 9.4 percent (357) of Opportunity Zone census tracts, the third quarter of 2026 marked the highest median home value since the beginning of the Great Recession in 2008 and 27.1 percent of the Opportunity Zone census tracts experienced double-digit growth in home values year-over-year. “Opportunity Zones remain a notably lower-cost segment of the housing market, with nearly 80 percent of these areas posting median home prices below the national median,” said Rob Barber, CEO of ATTOM. “Even so , home values were only slightly less likely to rise in these areas in the third quarter, suggesting that many of these communities are still moving broadly with the market.” The national median home sales price in the third quarter was $368,000. Inside Opportunity Zones, 79.5 percent of census tracts in ATTOM’s analysis had typical home prices below the national median. Outside the zones, only 50.4 percent of census tracts in the analysis had typical prices below the national median. Due to the small number of sales in many Opportunity Zone census tracts, median price measurements can be volatile. The typical median sales price rose or fell by more than 5 percent quarter-over-quarter in 79.1 percent of the 3,431 tracts with sufficient data in the second and third quarters. Powering Real Estate Businesses with Property Data and Analytics Solutions For Every Industry Major findings from the report: Median single-family home and condo prices rose quarter-over-quarter in 48.1 percent (1,651) of the 3,431 Opportunity Zone census tracts with sufficient data in both the second and third quarter. Year-over-year, home prices rose in 48.9 percent (1,598) of the 3,265 Opportunity Zone census tracts with sufficient data in the third quarters of 2025 and 2026. Year-over-year, median home prices rose in 51.6 percent (28,212) of the 54,704 census tracts outside of Opportunity Zones with sufficient data in both quarters. Inside Opportunity Zones, 27.1 percent of tracts included in the analysis saw median home prices grow by at least 10 percent. Outside the zones, 29.4 percent of included tracts experienced at least double-digit growth. Among states with at least 25 Opportunity Zone census tracts with sufficient data to analyze, Maine had the largest share that experienced year-over-year median home price growth (64 percent), followed by South Carolina (61.3 percent), Wisconsin (58.3 percent), Virginia (53 percent), and Oregon (52.3 percent). ATTOM’s report incorporates ResiScores, AI-derived neighborhood rankings based on projected home price appreciation. Inside Opportunity Zones, 76 of the census tracts included in ATTOM’s analysis had ResiScores of 100, indicating that their housing markets were projected to perform better than most other census tracts in their respective metro areas. Conclusion ATTOM’s third quarter 2026 Opportunity Zones report showed that areas outside the zones experienced median home price growth at a greater rate than areas inside the zones and were more likely to see double-digit median home price increases. Report methodology The ATTOM Opportunity Zones analysis is based on home sales price data derived from recorded sales deeds. Statistics for previous quarters are revised when each new report is issued as more deed data becomes available. ATTOM’s analysis compared median home prices in census tracts designated as Opportunity Zones by the Internal Revenue Service. Except where noted, tracts were used for the analysis if they had at least five sales in the third quarter of 2026. Median household income data for tracts and counties comes from surveys taken by the U.S. Census Bureau ( www.census.gov ) from 2020 through 2024. The list of designated Qualified Opportunity Zones is located at U.S. Department of the Treasury . Regions are based on designations by the Census Bureau. Hawaii and Alaska, which the bureau designates as part of the Pacific region, were included in the West region for this report. The report also included a ResiScore for each tract with sufficient data. The AI-powered scores combine housing market indicators including trends, appreciation, acceleration, forecast strength, and volatility into a single number between 0 and 100 that indicates the relative strength of a census tract’s housing market compared to other tracts in the same metropolitan area. items.description: Mortgage Rates Primary Mortgage Market Survey ® (PMMS ® ) results are based on the mortgage rate collected from thousands of loan applications submitted to Freddie Mac through Loan Product Advisor ® (LPA ® ) from lenders across the country when a borrower applies for a mortgage. Learn more in our FAQs . Primary Mortgage Market Survey ® U.S. weekly mortgage rate averages as of 11/05/2026 30-year Fixed-Rate Mortgage 7.18% 15-year Fixed-Rate Mortgage 6.57% Download Rates Since 1971 Mortgage Rates Decline for Third Consecutive Week to 7.18% Mortgage rates continued their downward trajectory this week, improving the environment for prospective homebuyers against a backdrop of strong economic growth. The 30-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 7.18% as of November 5, 2026, down from last week when it averaged 7.24%. A year ago at this time, the 30-year FRM averaged 6.22%. The 15-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 6.57%, down from last week when it averaged 6.60%. A year ago at this time, the 15-year FRM averaged 5.50%. PMMS results are released weekly on Thursdays at 12 p.m. ET. and are an average of loan rates offered the prior Thursday through Wednesday. See our publication calendar . Compare Historical PMMS Results Frequently Asked Questions Toggle all accordion sections Expand All What data is used for PMMS? The PMMS results are based on data from our Loan Product Advisor (LPA): mortgage rates collected from thousands of loan applications submitted to Freddie Mac from lenders across the country when a borrower applies for a mortgage. For more detailed information, see Enhanced Mortgage Rate Survey Explained . How is the national average determined? We collect the mortgage rate of all purchase applications based on PMMS criteria and a national average mortgage rate is calculated out of all the selected loan applications. The criteria include weekly conventional, single-family originations with conforming loan limits as set by FHFA. Is the PMMS rate based on current lender quotes or recent settlements? PMMS rates are based on applications submitted to Freddie Mac for the given week from lenders across the country. What type of lenders are included in the PMMS? Currently, our lenders are a mix of credit unions, commercial banks and mortgage lending companies. Do the PMMS results represent the rates charged on a specific day of the week? If so, which day? Or are they the average rate charged that week? PMMS is published each Thursday at noon ET. When a U.S. holiday falls on a Thursday, the PMMS will publish on the Wednesday of that week. The week of application activity starts at 12:00 a.m. ET the prior Thursday and lasts through 11:59 p.m. ET Wednesday. Therefore, the PMMS results are an average of loan rates offered Thursday through Wednesday. See our publication calendar . Why are adjustable rates no longer published? ARMs indexed to alternatives to U.S. Treasury securities have become more prevalent in the market. As we worked on enhancing the PMMS , we carefully considered which loan products were most popular for the PMMS borrower profile (good/excellent credit, 20% loans, home purchase loans on owner occupied 1-unit single-family properties). Additionally, in recent years the mortgage market has been dominated by fixed mortgage products. While there has been an uptick recently in the share of adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs) for the broader mortgage market, ARMs remain most popular for higher loan size (nonconforming) loans. Why are fees/points no longer published? Under the current LPA requirements, fees and points are not always required to be provided by lenders. Therefore, we are not able to report on the average fees and points. How has PMMS changed over time? Since April 1971, Freddie Mac shared the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rate with the PMMS. We have updated the information we collect and the process for gathering data over time. Changes in Data Processes When it was launched, PMMS surveyed lenders on the rates and points for their most popular 30-year fixed-rate, 15-year fixed-rate and 5/1 hybrid amortizing adjustable-rate mortgage products. The survey was based on first-lien prime conventional conforming home purchase mortgages with a loan-to-value of 80 percent. In addition, the adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) products were indexed to U.S. Treasury yields, and lenders were asked for both the initial coupon rate and points as well as the margin on the ARM products. Lenders surveyed each week were a mix of lender types — credit unions, commercial banks and mortgage lending companies — roughly proportional to the level of mortgage business that each type commands nationwide. On November 17, 2022, the mortgage rate gathering process was updated. Instead of surveying lenders, we now use data from our Loan Product Advisor (LPA). Changes in Information Shared In 1984 , the 1-year ARM was added to the survey. In 1991 , the 15-year fixed-rate mortgage rate was added. In January 2005 , a 5/1 hybrid ARM series was added. In January 2016 , the 1-year ARM was discontinued. In November 2022 , adjustable rates and fees/points were discontinued. For more detailed information, see Enhanced Mortgage Rate Survey Explained . items.title: Safest and riskiest places to live in the U.S. 2050
items.description: Safety has a price, and it will be paid. Cotality analyzed the top 10 safest and riskiest places to live in the U.S. and found that the areas or the country that are least vulnerable to natural catastrophes are also where prices are growing the fastest. In all states, the cost of homeownership is no longer calculated by mortgage payments alone. As the risk of natural disasters increases, insuring a home is increasingly determining the final monthly cost of being a homeowner. At the same time, people are paying more to live in regions where natural catastrophes are of less concern. Pennsylvania recorded some of the most pronounced year-over-year home price growth in August 2026. Arizona and the District of Columbia are poised to see the most price growth in the coming year, according to Cotality’s Home Price Index. These states will also be some of the safest come 2050. Rebuilding a home is a financial burden across all points of the industry. Lenders worry about mortgage payments. Insurers face portfolio profitability concerns. Homeowners can enter the classic default hierarchy: depleting emergency savings, maxing out credit cards, and tapping short-term debt before their financial cushion evaporates and they risk default. items.title: Multifamily Developer Confidence Weakens in Third Quarter
items.description: Multifamily Developer Confidence Weakens in Third Quarter November 5, 2026 Eric Lynch No Comments New multifamily housing confidence weakened year-over-year in the third quarter, according to the Multifamily Market Survey (MMS) by the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB). The MMS produces two separate indices. The Multifamily Production Index (MPI) had a reading of 41, down five points year-over-year, while the Multifamily Occupancy Index (MOI) had a reading of 69, also down five points year-over-year. Developer sentiment for new multifamily production has softened, due to challenges such as high interest rates , construction costs that are high relative to rents, and problems getting projects approved and connected to roads and utilities, resulting in many projects taking longer to complete. Due to the headwinds facing the industry, NAHB’s 2027 forecast shows a decline for multifamily starts. Although the administration’s regulatory reform efforts are helping to ease some cost pressures, the multifamily sector would still benefit from an expedited permit process and lower rates on development and construction loans . Multifamily Production Index (MPI) The MMS asks multifamily developers to rate the current conditions as “good ”, “fair”, or “poor” for multifamily starts in markets where they are active. The index and all its components are scaled so that a number above 50 indicates that more respondents report conditions as good rather than poor. The MPI is a weighted average of four key market segments: three in the built-for-rent market (garden/low-rise, mid/high-rise, and subsidized) and the built-for-sale (or condominium) market. All four components experienced decreases year-over-year and are in negative territory (i.e., below 50) during the third quarter. The component measuring subsidized units fell six points to 49, the component measuring garden/low-rise dropped five points to 48, and both the component measuring mid/high-rise units and the component measuring built-for-sale units decreased four points to 33 and 31, respectively. Multifamily Occupancy Index (MOI) The survey also asks multifamily property owners to rate the current conditions for occupancy of existing rental apartments in markets where they are active as “good”, “fair”, or “poor”. Like the MPI, the MOI and all its components are scaled so that a number above 50 indicates more respondents report that occupancy is good than poor. The MOI is a weighted average of three built-for-rent market segments (garden/low-rise, mid/high-rise, and subsidized). Two of the three components experienced declines year-over-year for the third quarter of 2026. The mid/high-rise component declined seven points to 59 and the garden/low-rise component fell six points to 70. The component measuring subsidized units saw an increase of two points to 83. Nevertheless, all three components remained above the break-even point of 50. Changes in Overall Market Conditions The MMS was re-designed in 2023 to produce results that are easier to interpret and consistent with the proven format of other NAHB industry sentiment surveys. Until there is enough data to seasonally adjust the series, changes in the MMS indices should only be evaluated on a year-over-year basis. For more recent information about the market, the survey contains a separate question asking multifamily developers to compare current market conditions to conditions three months earlier. In the third quarter of 2026, 6% of respondents said the current market is better, and 28% said it is worse. However, the majority of developers—66%—said that the market is currently about the same as it was three months ago. Please visit NAHB’s MMS web page for the full report. Economic uncertainty, geopolitical disruption, shifting workforce expectations, and rapid technological advancement are forcing organizations to rethink not only where they operate, but how location decisions support broader business priorities. To better understand these shifts, Colliers partnered with CoreNet Global to survey more than 140 corporate real estate professionals from around the world. The findings reveal that location strategy has evolved from a transactional real estate function into a strategic business discipline sitting at the intersection of talent, growth, resilience, and operational performance. Talent still leads, but the definition of ‘talent market' is changing Talent remains a primary driver of location decisions. Growth expectations shift toward Asia Pacific Asia Pacific was identified as the region most likely to experience net new portfolio growth over the next three to five years (52%), followed by North America (30%). The report notes that organizations continue to view Asia Pacific as a key destination for expansion, while North America remains an important market for growth, investment, and business activity. Location strategy has evolved as an enterprise decision Respondents identified revenue growth, AI and automation adoption, cost reduction, and talent acquisition and retention among the leading business priorities influencing decision-making over the next 24 months. Other key priorities include improving employee experience and supporting business growth. Confidence remains high despite rising complexity More than two-thirds of respondents reported being very or somewhat confident in their organization's ability to make long-term location decisions despite ongoing change and uncertainty. Open-ended responses highlighted recurring concerns around cost pressures, market volatility, talent availability, geopolitical risk, and the need for future flexibility. items.title: Homebuyers Get Some Relief as Prices Decline For Third Straight Week, Monthly Payments Dip
items.description: Homebuyers Get Some Relief as Prices Decline For Third Straight Week, Monthly Payments Dip Published on November 5th, 2026 by Dana Anderson New listings of homes for sale fell to their lowest level since the start of the year, but there are still significantly more sellers than buyers in the market. What to know about the U.S. housing market for the four weeks ending November 1: Prices fell for the third week in a row. The median home-sale price was $388,604, down 0.4% year over year. That marks the third straight week in which prices declined after three years of increases. Monthly payments dropped to a 5-week low. The median monthly mortgage payment was $2,777, down from a peak of $2,811 in early October. This data is seasonally adjusted. Costs declined because mortgage rates and sale prices are slowly coming down. House hunting activity declined. Pending home sales fell 0.6% week over week to the lowest level in records dating back to 2021. Sellers pulled back, too. New listings dropped 1.5% from a week earlier to the lowest level since January, as would-be sellers reacted to slow demand. The slow market is giving buyers room to negotiate. The buyers who are out there may be able to negotiate prices down and/or get other concessions from sellers. Buyers have more homes to choose from than a year ago, and less competition: There are 2.1% more homes on the market than a year ago, while homes are taking a bit longer to sell. items.title: HELOC originations up 20%: Lead with equity as refis stall
items.description: HELOC originations up 20%: Lead with equity as refis stall By Colin McNamara Published November 05, 2026, 10:20 a.m. EST | Updated November 05, 2026, 11:01 a.m. EST 2 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Expert Quote: "Home equity demand should remain relatively resilient, supported by several quarters of steady HELOC growth." — Satyan Merchant, Senior Vice President, TransUnion Supporting Data: HELOCs accounted for more than half of all home equity activity in the second quarter. Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. As interest rates remain elevated , borrowers are searching for solutions that unlock home equity without requiring a mortgage refinance. Processing Content Home equity originations increased 10.1% year over year to 757,000 in the second quarter, with home equity line of credit originations rising 20.3%, according to TransUnion's Q3 2026 Credit Industry Insights Report. HELOCs accounted for more than half of all home equity activity. "Homeowners are increasingly turning to home equity products as a way to access cash without giving up the low rates on their primary mortgage," Satyan Merchant, senior vice president, automotive and mortgage business leader at TransUnion, told National Mortgage News. "Demand is likely to remain strongest for HELOCs, which offer flexible, on-demand access to equity while preserving existing first-lien financing." Satyan Merchant, senior vice president, automotive and mortgage business leader at TransUnion Mortgage originations as a whole jumped 12.8% on an annual basis to 1.5 million in the second quarter, as lower rates supported stronger activity. Refinance volume rose about 40%, increasing its share of total originations to 21.5% from 17.4% a year earlier. Rate-and-term refinances led the spike, jumping nearly 60%, according to the report. But interest rates rose above last year's levels for much of the third quarter and all of the fourth quarter so far, which Merchant expects to sideline homebuyers and subdue activity. The 30-year fixed rate mortgage has fallen recently, down to 7.24% last week, but it remains more than a percentage point above the same week last year, according to Freddie Mac. "However, home equity demand should remain relatively resilient, supported by several quarters of steady HELOC growth as homeowners continue to tap accumulated equity rather than refinance into higher-rate mortgages," Merchant added. Finance of America's third quarter earnings further portrayed this. The reverse mortgage lender's funded volume increased 24% year over year and 2% from the second quarter while the rest of the industry struggled to combat high rates. Mortgage performance was generally stable, although serious delinquency rates continued to normalize from historically low pandemic-era levels. The percentage of borrowers 60 or more days delinquent reached 1.64% in the third quarter. The increases concentrated primarily among Federal Housing Administration loans, which now represent nearly half of all seriously delinquent mortgage accounts. Performance on other loan types, including Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac and jumbo, were steady. "Looking ahead, interest rates will continue to shape purchase and refinance demand," Merchant said. "At the same time, home equity products may remain an important source of liquidity for borrowers seeking to preserve their low mortgage rates." items.title: Florida’s Amendment 3 could give housing market a ‘sugar high’ through year-end
items.description: Jason Haber, a Compass broker licensed in both Florida and New York, believes the Sunshine State’s approval of Amendment 3 will lead to the state’s housing market experiencing a “sugar high” to close out the year. Amendment 3 , which was approved by 62% of the electorate on Tuesday, easily surpassing the 60% threshold, increases the homestead exemption, reducing the taxable value of a person's primary residence in the state. Prior to this, homeowners could receive an exemption of up to $50,000, but the amendment increases the exemption on non-school property taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. Beyond that, the amendment says the exemption will be adjusted for inflation. This means that if someone's primary residence has an assessed value of $350,000, in 2028, the new $250,000 exemption would leave $100,000 subject to non-school property taxes, assuming the homeowner qualifies for the full exemption, generating potentially thousands of dollars in savings for homeowners. Haber agrees that the amendment could create “serious property tax savings for those who homestead in Florida.” “That was clearly very attractive to the majority of people. Affordability is the top domestic issue of our time right now and people see this as direct relief on their cost of living,” Haber said. Carrots to entice people to move to the Sunshine State But the amendment comes with a caveat. Homeowners must establish primary residency in Florida before Dec. 31, 2026, in order to be eligible for the 2027 and 2028 exemptions. If you establish primary residency after the deadline, you will have to wait five years until you're eligible for the expanded exemptions, which is why Haber believes the market may experience a “sugar high.” “If you were on the fence this would certainly move you to act quickly,” Haber said, noting that Florida uses a variety of “carrots” to entice people to move to the state. Chris Wands, the founder of The Wands Team , a RealTrends Verified ranked team, at Douglas Elliman , a RealTrends Verified brokerage, shares a similar view. “It may make people move faster especially if they are already planning to move in the first half of next year,” Wands said. “I think it makes Florida an even more attractive state. A lot of people are moving here for the tax benefits, so adding another benefit helps with that.” If a “sugar high” market does happen, local real estate professionals said it could have greater impacts on some markets than others. “In Boca Raton right now, if a house is priced properly, you will have six people fighting over it, but that isn’t the case in every market. Further north in the state, the market is weaker because those markets are more impacted by high interest rates, so it would be a different story there," Haber said. Danielle Blake, the chief of residential and advocacy at Miami Realtors + RWorld , shares a similar view. “Availability of inventory is going to vary by the asset class that you are looking for, whether it is single family or condominiums, and also the geographic location. In Miami, we have more condo inventory than single-family inventory at affordable price points, but that also varies by cities. Some cities have a larger supply, so it really varies,” Blake said. In addition to a potential uptick in new residents, Wands also believes this could impact current primary residents’ decisions on purchasing larger properties, especially if they were previously concerned about how property taxes could impact their long-term affordability. This could then open up more mid-level or entry-level properties, helping more people get into the housing market. Blake however, is skeptical, noting that despite this impacting the property tax portion of the affordability equation, many current homeowners may be reluctant to give up the 3% mortgage rate they have on their current property, especially in today’s mortgage rate environment. In addition to this, property taxes in Florida are reset when a property is sold, meaning that if the purchase price goes up, so do the property taxes. “Even if you're not paying as much as you otherwise would have, anything that pushes up purchase price and, by extension, property taxes can have that adverse impact on affordability,” Haber said. Additionally, legislators could increase the millage rate, which would hamper the affordability benefits homeowners are hoping to gain out of this amendment. Perks for renters Beyond impacting homeowners, Wands also noted the amendment’s provisions relating to investment properties could also help renters. Under Amendment 3, the annual cap on increases in the assessed value of non-homestead properties drops from 10% to 5%. This means that if a rental property's assessed value is $300,000, the existing 10% cap would generally allow its assessed value to increase by as much as $30,000 in a year. Under the new 5% cap, that increase would be limited to $15,000. “I think it puts guard rails up for renters and investment property owners by giving them more stability in what they can expect their taxes to be,” Wands said. The New York to Florida pipeline If Florida sees an influx of homebuyers set on establishing their primary residency prior to the Dec. 31, 2026 cut off, it would naturally have an impact on other housing markets as the buyers have to come from somewhere. Unsurprisingly, many are pointing to New York City as a market that could be impacted by the amendment’s approval. “The year-end residency cut off is going to bring a lot of decisions,” Frances Katzen, the founder of The Katzen Team , a RealTrends Verified team, at Douglas Elliman, said. I’m going to be watching for people who are going to downsize their primary home here, keeping a small apartment as a base, but moving their primary residence to Florida. items.title: ULI Emerging Trends Report: Manhattan, Jersey City, Among Top 10 Markets to Watch in 2027
items.description: ULI Emerging Trends Report: Manhattan, Jersey City, Among Top 10 Markets to Watch in 2027 by Taylor Williams November 5, 2026 November 5, 2026 4 LAS VEGAS — Ranking No. 7 and No. 8, respectively, Manhattan and Jersey City are both among the Top 10 markets to watch in terms of overall real estate prospects, according to the Emerging Trends in Real Estate 202 7 report, which is jointly produced every year by the Urban Land Institute (ULI) and accounting firm PwC. No other Northeast cities or municipalities cracked the Top 20, although the Northern New Jersey region as a whole secured the No. 15 spot. According to the report’s authors, Manhattan’s ranking represents major improvement in real estate fundamentals across numerous asset classes; the borough ranked as low as 42nd in 2022. More specifically, the report stated that “Manhattan’s recovery is among the most diversified of the profiled markets, with simultaneous strengthening across [the] office, retail and tourism [sectors] and a substantial infrastructure pipeline that reinforces the market’s long-term competitive position.” As the largest U.S. office market by inventory, Manhattan has always had the toughest road to recovery in the post-COVID era. However, absorption found a fresh catalyst in 2025 and 2026 in the form of AI [artificial intelligence] companies, which accounted for 2.8 million square feet of leasing activity in 2026 alone and 3.8 million square feet over the past two years. The borough’s housing market remain notoriously supply-constrained, having only added about 7,500 new units since 2025. Jersey City took home the silver medal in last year’s rankings thanks in large part to a massive volume of new multifamily construction starts and deliveries. With scores of new units coming on line and new projects still penciling, Jersey City remains a low[er]-cost alternative to Manhattan that retains its ease of connectivity to the country’s business and financial hub, as well as its own unique food-and-beverage and nightlife scenes. items.title: What the midterm results mean for multifamily
items.description: What the midterm results mean for multifamily Housing affordability is likely to remain a top priority for Congress as Democrats take control, experts said. Published Nov. 5, 2026 Julie Strupp Senior Editor Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google Bill Pugliano via Getty Images Listen to the article 6 min This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback . Housing affordability was a defining issue in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, and it will likely remain a priority in the upcoming Democratic-controlled Congress, experts said. Democrats clinched majorities in both the House and Senate and flipped several governor’s seats, CNBC reported. Both sides care deeply about housing, and the affordability challenge is not going away, Greg Brown, the National Apartment Association’s senior vice president of government affairs, told Multifamily Dive. That shared priority was evident when Democrats and Republicans came together this summer to pass the most consequential federal housing legislation in decades, as well as in “the conversations that we've already had with members of Congress from both sides about what comes next,” on housing policy, Brown said. But it will be “interesting to see how [that process] plays out, given the new division of control.” Congressional committee members worked across the aisle to pass the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act , and that could offer a model for getting more housing legislation approved, Andy Winkler, managing director for housing and infrastructure at the Bipartisan Policy Center, told Multifamily Dive. Part of the reason that ROAD passed “was Congress had not done that much related to housing over the last few years, and yet we've seen such staggering housing costs, and so they really did feel the pressure to respond,” Winkler said. It will take time for new congressmembers to staff up and get up to speed on issues, Winkler said, “which creates this real need for stakeholders and others to engage and educate members and staff about housing and their priorities.” One major complaint from the multifamily industry is that national politicians are focused on homeownership and don’t pay as much attention to the rental housing industry, Bernard Fulton, senior vice president of legislative and political affairs for the National Multifamily Housing Council, told Multifamily Dive. Although both parties recognize that more housing action is needed, “just because they think this is something that has to be addressed doesn't necessarily mean they have the right path forward,” Fulton said. “And that's [the multifamily industry’s] opportunity.” New Congress brings changes Based on results of the last two major national elections, Fulton thinks elected officials have a lot more urgency to cut a deal. He expects to see tariff and tax legislation coming out of Congress, as well as more oversight of the financial regulators that influence interest rates. “I fully expect once we really get into the nitty-gritty of January for people to immediately start introducing bills, and start crafting even a second comprehensive ROAD 2.0, maybe even before the end of 2027, [send it] to the White House,” Fulton said. Democratic control of both houses could lead to national budgets that protect federal programs like Community Development Block Grants and the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit , which also aid the expansion of affordable multifamily housing, Joel Berner, senior economist with Realtor.com, told Multifamily Dive in emailed comments. Other key issues to watch are whether areas “where Democrats gained power choose to pursue rent control or other tenant protections, how immigration policy changes and what effects it might have on the construction labor force, and whether Democrats at the federal level work to roll back tariffs on construction materials," Berner said. Big changes are coming to the House Financial Services Committee, which has authority over HUD, the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s housing programs and some of the financial regulators, according to Fulton. “We see pretty significant people not returning to those committees, and you also have new committee leadership in the House,” he said. Republicans have been very focused on deregulatory measures and streamlining some HUD programs, according to Winkler, but “where maybe their priorities shift is if Congress changes the funding or appropriations levels or anything else.” Winkler expects additional scrutiny on how agencies are implementing ROAD. Most of the programs and changes that the bill creates are not funded and will require appropriations, and “I do think maybe in a Democrat-controlled House and Senate, the dynamics of funding some of those programs could be different,” Winkler said. More collaboration on housing ahead? Despite party differences, housing still seems like an area ripe for collaboration in the new Congress, Winkler said. “I do think if you're looking at divided government in which the bills that a Democratically controlled Congress passes need to be signed by the president to become law, this is one area that stands out to me as an opportunity to continue to work on the progress that was made this Congress,” Winkler said. There's increasingly a broad recognition that the root of the housing problem is a lack of supply, according to Fulton. items.title: James Stewart Biopic Jimmy Premieres in Fort Worth
items.description: Live Poll Arlington screenwriter Justin Strawhand became inspired by the subtle whiff of gasoline fumes while huddled with his laptop at a café table underneath the nose of a B-24 at Dallas Executive Airport . And he was galvanized by the historic significance of the former Hotel Texas in downtown Fort Worth, where he locked himself in a room while completing his first draft. That ineffable connection became vital to discovering some of the nuances in Jimmy , a biopic revolving around actor James Stewart’s military service during World War II and how it impacted his life and career. “I was trying to find some sort of spiritual connection with Jimmy,” says Strawhand, who relocated from New Jersey to North Texas about five years ago. “Jimmy loved it down here. It felt like he had this huge heart here and I could shadow some of the places he had been.” The film screened during the opening night of the 20th Lone Star Film Festival on Nov. 4 in Fort Worth and opens in theaters on Nov. 6. Strawhand already was a Stewart fan before filmmaker Aaron Burns sent him a magazine feature story that detailed the years between Stewart earning an Academy Award in 1940 for The Philadelphia Story and his next major starring role six years later in It’s a Wonderful Life . During much of that gap, Stewart (played in the film by Riverdale star K.J. Apa) served as a B-24 bomber pilot in the U.S. Army Air Corps, flying 20 combat missions over Europe and rising to the rank of colonel before returning home afflicted with PTSD. Arts Party Like It's 1949 at the Forest Theater The Forest Theater, which once played host to Prince and B.B. King, was nearly demolished to make way for a gas station. But after a decade-long effort, the South Dallas marquee shines again. By Bethany Erickson | October 29, 2026 | 10:09 am “I found Stewart’s transformation during that period — he won an Oscar and three months later he’s enlisting — fascinating in how it takes him down to the bottom emotionally,” Burns says. “He found healing and hope and purpose. He’s a human and he’s broken, but he found his peace and his joy.” Debuting the film in Fort Worth became a no-brainer, given Stewart’s affection for the area. After filming a few sequences of the 1955 war drama Strategic Air Command at Carswell Air Force Base, he returned to narrate a 1970s promotional film and became an ambassador for the Fort Worth Zoo. Production on Jimmy took place in September 2025 primarily in Ireland, where the filmmakers re-created both the period European locales and 1940s Hollywood. They also shot for one day at Dallas Executive, capturing some interior B-24 footage to go with the exterior replica on set. One goal became not allowing any budget or logistical constraints to compromise the project’s historical or narrative accuracy. “He was very famous but decides to put that fame on hold and serve his country at great personal risk. He’s flying planes over Berlin, not sitting on the sidelines. He comes back to Hollywood and is basically forgotten because he’s been away for so long,” Strawhand says. “His last chance was this crazy script that [director] Frank Capra gave him.” That script, of course, was It’s a Wonderful Life , the beloved holiday perennial that — given the timing for Stewart personally — was perhaps more meaningful than any other film in his distinguished career. “It’s really about the creation of Jimmy Stewart through the cauldron of war,” Strawhand says. “Jimmy invents a really authentic type of acting in It’s a Wonderful Life . It’s not method acting. Jimmy bleeds on the screen. That’s why we still watch it.” Burns wasn’t interested in hero worship or iconic hagiography. But in Stewart’s case, he says the actor’s enduring legacy is defined by his uncommon relatability. “He left behind him a trail of kindness,” Burns says. “As a Hollywood celebrity, he could have been whoever he wanted. He chose to become George Bailey.” Read Next Film Is There A Role For AI in Filmmaking? Dallas filmmakers and festival directors weigh in on the most polarizing topic of our day. items.title: Democrats Will Focus on Affordability in 2027, Party Leaders Say
items.description: Democrats rode affordability anxieties to big wins in the midterm elections. But they must deliver on lowering costs if they want to sustain their political power, Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) said Thursday. Speaking at a Washington, DC, forum hosted by Center for American Progress, a left-leaning think tank, Schumer reflected on the significant gains in Tuesday's midterm elections. Democrats were able to flip dozens of seats and gain control of both the House and Senate for the upcoming Congress. Democrats spent the year attacking President Donald Trump on "costs, chaos, and corruption," as Schumer put it. But although many people voted for Democrats out of frustration with the Trump administration, that doesn't mean they're enthusiastic about the Democratic Party, he conceded. "We highlighted how Trump's chaos agenda was causing Americans pain at the grocery store, at the gas pump," Schumer said. "Every month in the spring, we focused on the costs of the American people and what we were going to do about it." Vice President JD Vance has also said that the conflict in Iran and subsequent inflation surge cost Republicans the election. Schumer said Democrats have to bring down costs . Ending the Iran conflict and stopping the tariffs policies that have driven up costs in the country are two ways to do that. Although Democrats made major gains, they still won't have enough votes to override a Trump veto. And Democratic leadership will have to find common ground with the party's left flank after a wave of Democratic Socialist candidates won elections on Tuesday, a fact Schumer acknowledged without mentioning the group by name. "Unity means linking arms with people you will not agree with on every issue so you can make progress on the more important areas where you agree," Schumer said. "Intra-party debate isn't a sign of weakness." Wealth of ideas Democrats who won state and local races have promised affordability-minded reforms and emphasized housing production . That's crucial in expensive areas such as California and Washington DC. Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker said at the CAP event that medical and student debt are also issues Democrats should tackle at the federal level. These debts significantly delay homeownership . But he said both oversight and affordability should be Congress' main focus next year. "You can walk and chew gum, we have to deal with affordability, that has to be the principal thing," Pritzer said. "But we have to have oversight committees, just like the Republicans did." On Wednesday, New York Rep. Hakeem Jeffries , who is likely to become the new speaker of the House, said the House Democratic Caucus will convene next week and lay out an agenda. But Democrats would focus on "affordability and accountability" with their new majority, he said. Loading... "We're going to fight hard for the heartland of America," New York Rep. Hakeem Jefferies, who is likely to become the new speaker of the House, said Wednesday. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images Democrats after the election threw out a host of ideas for items to pursue in 2027 and 2028. Many of them focused on both affordability and guardrails for artificial intelligence and data centers. "Top of the Democratic agenda on day 1 needs to be a pause on advanced AI development, regulation of this out of control industry, and a ban on artificial superintelligence," Rep. Yassamin Ansari (D-AZ) posted to X on Wednesday. The Nasdaq plunged 5% the next day, led by a sharp decline in tech stocks. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT), who caucuses with the Democrats, called for a national 5% wealth tax in a video message Thursday morning. Such a tax, as is being considered in California, could fund 7 million units of affordable housing, Sanders said. Lost spending power Realtor.com® economists quantified just how bad the affordability situation is for Americans. In January, a $2,000 monthly mortgage payment supported a home price $28,500 higher than a year earlier. By October 2026, that same payment supported a home price $33,600 lower. The surge in interest rates, from 6.05% in February to 7.33% in October, was to blame for the $62,100 swing. “Mortgage rates are not abstract to a family trying to buy a home,” says Danielle Hale , chief economist at Realtor.com. “They show up as the home they can no longer afford." "The year-over-year comparison is a vivid measure of why housing affordability lands as a pocketbook issue for voters," Hale continues. "The conflict’s inflationary impact is one source of uncertainty, but households feel the consequences in their monthly budgets and in the homes they have to take off their list.” In a post, National Association of Homebuilders Chief Advocacy Officer Ken Wingert urged the next Congress to craft more housing bills like the comprehensive 21st Century Road to Housing Act that passed this summer. Lawmakers have suggested they have their own sets of ideas for new housing measures to pursue. Cities and localities, they have said, must also step up to implement new laws. Those rules must assuage builders whose confidence has been shattered by high costs of building materials and high mortgage rates chasing homebuyers out of the market. The National Association of Home Builders/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index (HMI) fell to a 14-year low last month. "With a national housing shortfall of roughly 1.2 million households, more must be done to let builders build—and voters agree," Wingert said. "Throughout the campaign, voters consistently cited housing availability and affordability as key factors in their decisions." items.title: Los Angeles Mayor-Elect Nithya Raman Vows To Triple Homebuilding To Improve Affordability
items.description: Los Angeles City Councilmember Nithya Raman has unseated the city's Democrat incumbent Mayor Karen Bass after running a campaign centered on affordability and housing. The Associated Press called the election for Raman on Thursday afternoon as she widened her lead over Bass. Bass, 73, called Raman to concede her loss and congratulate her successor on her victory. "While this is not the outcome we hoped for, the people of Los Angeles have spoken," the outgoing mayor said in a statement, in part. "I have committed to ensuring a smooth and seamless transition. Moving this city forward is what Los Angeles needs from all of us." The win underscored a "blue wave" that swept Democrats into control of both chambers of Congress , delivering a decisive rebuke to President Donald Trump and the Republican Party. When Raman, 45, takes office in January, L.A. will become the nation's second-largest city led by a democratic socialist, following in the footsteps of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani . Raman's swearing-in will expand a growing roster of democratic socialist mayors nationwide, including Janeese Lewis George in Washington, DC , Katie Wilson in Seattle , and David Morales, in Providence, RI. Ahead of her victory, Raman appeared before a jubilant crowd of supporters at the Greek Theatre Plaza in Griffith Park Tuesday, arguing that L.A. voters were frustrated with Bass' record on cost of living and were demanding change, reported KTLA5 . "We watched friend after friend, family after family, leave because they couldn’t afford to stay here anymore. And we all talked about it as if these things were completely out of City Hall’s control," she told the audience. "That’s the cynicism that started to take over this city. That started to make us believe that L.A.’s problems weren't just bad, but they were permanent." A platform focused on housing Raman ran a campaign focusing on housing, homelessness, and safety issues. The centerpiece of her platform was a plan to triple annual housing production by speeding up permitting through strict "shot clocks" for approvals. Further proposals included overhauling inspections, updating codes, and eliminating additional fees to incentivize developers to build more starter homes. Loading... Raman, right, has been critical of Mayor Bass' record on housing and affordability. Los Angeles Daily News via Getty Images ""oday, less than 10% of the new homes built in L.A. are for-sale," Raman recently told Realtor.com®. "Under current city and state regulations, for-sale projects are charged higher fees, have a more-complicated approval process, are easier to appeal, and have increased liability risks for developers." The 43-year-old councilmember was sharply critical of her mayoral predecessor, contending that Bass has not done enough to tackle L.A.’s yearslong housing crisis. Bass’ record includes signing Executive Directive 1, which streamlined approval for roughly 50,000 units of fully affordable housing, overseeing a historic rezoning program to clear a path for building half a million new homes, adding more housing units to transit corridors and job hubs, simplifying the building application process, and updating rent stabilization rules for the first time in 40 years to shield tenants from steep hikes. However, it was on Bass’ watch that Realtor.com Metro Report Cards released in September ranked L.A. the nation’s least affordable large city—a result that Raman did not find surprising. "We’ve made it too difficult, time consuming, and costly to build homes in Los Angeles," concluded Raman. Assuming a 10% down payment and a 6.5% 30-year fixed mortgage, a median earner in L.A. would have to spend nearly 85% of their income on monthly mortgage payments on a $1.12 million median-priced home, effectively putting ownership out of reach of all but the wealthiest buyers. Beyond cost-of-living issues, Raman face pressure upon taking office to deliver on her lofty campaign pledge to reduce citywide homelessness by 50% in time for the 2028 Summer Olympics in Los Angeles. Fulfilling that promise will be a major challenge, given that recent 2026 data showed roughly 45,000 people living in tents and encampments on the streets of L.A. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in New York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.

items.title: Simon Property Group Takes Out $93M Loan To Refinance Colorado Mills Mall
items.description: Wikimedia Commons/Jeffrey Beall Simon Property Group took out a $93M loan for Lakewood’s Colorado Mills mall, with $80M being sold into CMBS , according to a term sheet filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday. The loan, granted by Goldman Sachs and German American Capital Corp. , has an interest rate of approximately 6.84%. It is set to mature in November 2036, according to the SEC filing. Simon didn’t respond to multiple requests for comment from Bisnow . Colorado Mills is one of the largest shopping centers in the Denver metro. The 1.4M SF mall was built in 2002 and renovated after a ferocious 2017 hailstorm that seriously damaged the property and led to its temporary closure. It was 98% occupied as of Aug. 31, according to the SEC filing. The mall added Cavender’s Boot City as a new tenant earlier this month. In early 2025, Colorado Mills was reappraised at $135M, 37% less than its 2014 valuation. Simon took out a $117.7M loan in 2014 that was transferred to special servicing before its November 2024 maturity date, Bisnow previously reported . In May 2025, after the property was reappraised, Simon avoided default on the loan by securing a two-year extension deal . Colorado Mills’ net operating income has fluctuated over the years, but the property appears to be performing better this year. Its net operating income through the first seven months of 2026 was about $18.7M, up nearly $1.3M from last year, according to the SEC filing. Colorado Mills’ $80M CMBS loan is part of an $805M pool with 63 commercial mortgage loans backed by 79 properties across the U.S. The local mall’s loan is the largest in the pool, accounting for about 10%, Kroll Bond Rating Agency said in a statement. Malls across the country have faced shifting market conditions over the past decade. The number of malls in the U.S. dropped from 2,500 in the 1980s to 700 in 2024. Despite the closures, malls are now the “top performer in commercial real estate,” with values increasing 13% year-over-year, The Wall Street Journal reported . Park Meadows mall in Lone Tree also faced a potential default in 2024. The mall’s owner, Brookfield Properties, refinanced by securing a $700M loan with a five-year term just days before its previous $615M property loan matured. items.title: Ellington eyes non-QM servicing growth in new acquisition
items.description: Ellington eyes non-QM servicing growth in new acquisition By Spencer Lee CloseText About Spencer twitter Spencer_NYC linkedin spencer-lee-journo Published November 05, 2026, 2:56 p.m. EST | Updated November 05, 2026, 3:52 p.m. EST 3 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Ellington Financial believes its new servicer acquisition presents it with opportunity to stand out in the specialized, growing segments it operates in and holds potential to attract future customers also active in the space. Processing Content The real estate investment trust announced its purchase this week of Statebridge Co., a diversified loan servicer, whose expertise primarily covers late-stage distress, along with residential-transition and other non-qualified mortgages . The move points to the diversification strategy occurring across mortgage businesses of all types, in response to changing expectations in origination mix and borrower performance over the coming months. The decision to acquire a servicer came about, in part, from industry contraction, which made it challenging for Ellington to find a partner that could effectively work with the types of delinquent and non-QM loans it owns. The company hinted at the likely merger over the summer in its second-quarter earnings. "We didn't see great options where we could really get what we think are best-in-class protocols, and have a dialog and be able to use our data analysis and our kind of native experience and expertise in the product to effectuate outcomes," said Ellington Co-Chief Investment Officer Mark Tecotzky on Thursday in its latest earnings call. While leaders advised that financial benefits might not appear on the balance sheet immediately, the upside would come in the longer term. "We're going to build this into the premier special servicer," added CEO Larry Penn. "Even with what we see as the delinquency pipeline now, once we've built this, I think there'll be plenty of business for Statebridge to grow and thrive on." As of September 30, Statebridge serviced approximately 14,700 loans representing an approximate unpaid principal balance of $1.9 billion, nearly all for third-party clients. The portfolio includes 3,500 non-QM and RTL loans, with balances totaling $1.1 billion, as well as a smaller subset of agency and commercial mortgages. With the attention now paid to the non-QM segment, the need to understand the nuances of those particular types of loans will also give Statebridge an advantage, Tecotzky explained. "Delinquencies when non-QM first started were trivially small," he said, noting the effect of Covid-era home-price appreciation on the housing market. "We don't see that HPA tailwind right now obviously, so we think long-term delinquencies will tick up to levels that are more consistent with reasonable expectations." "As we build this out, and we demonstrate the quality of the resolutions we believe Statebridge can get, others may want to use their services," Tecotzky continued. Ellington and Longbridge post "solid" third quarter The acquisition came in a third quarter when Ellington reported net income of $45.9 million, which represented a 20.9% decrease from the prior three-month period's $58 million. On a year-over-year basis, profit climbed 21.6% from $37.8 million. The bottom line numbers factored in results across its businesses, including its investment portfolio and reverse lending unit, Longbridge Financial, as well as changes in fair market value. "This was a solid quarter for EFC, against a market backdrop that has a lot more landmines than in the first half of the year," Tecotzky said. The portfolio investment arm was able to price two non-QM securitizations and a single agency-eligible transaction early in the quarter before spreads widened, he noted. With increased interest in non-QM and non-agency loans, the pace of such deals is approaching $5 billion a week, Ellington officials also noted. Interest rate pressures, though, led the company to introduce a sequential pay structure to address investor concerns about reduced refinance incentive. "Other non-QM issuers quickly adopted that approach," Tecotzky said. Net income at the Longbridge subsidiary came in at $12.5 million, 58.8% below the second-quarter's $30.2 million. Compared to a year ago, the reverse-lending business increased its profit by 4.5% from $8.6 million. Longbridge celebrated originations of $676.3 million during the third quarter, with volume rising 36% from the same three months in 2025. From July to September, the company grew its share of government-backed Home Equity Conversion Mortgage transactions to a record 31%, making it the second-largest issuer in the market. Meanwhile, among its proprietary offerings , September proved to be the strongest month ever for the products. "If anything, we're hoping for and expecting continued growth into next year," Penn said. "We do see the product continues to gain traction. Demographics are favorable, and I think the product makes a lot of sense. Obviously, we're broadening the product base as well." items.title: CFPB narrows enforcement practices, closes 86% of supervisory actions
items.description: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau ( CFPB ) said that it is narrowing its supervisory and enforcement activities and closing most of its outstanding supervisory actions, as well as pursuing changes to mortgage lending and servicing rules, according to its latest semi-annual report, released Oct. 27. The report, which covers the first half of 2026, outlines the bureau’s efforts to align its work with the Trump administration ’s priorities. During the broader reporting period of July 2025 through June 2026, the CFPB closed 1,327 of the 1,552 supervisory actions that were open as of July 1, 2025, or approximately 86%. The bureau said the closures reflected either institutions sufficiently addressing the issues or findings that no longer aligned with its priorities. The CFPB also reassessed all 80 open examinations and closed 66 that did not align with its revised priorities. The remaining 14 continued with a focus on correcting violations, addressing compliance weaknesses and providing relief to affected consumers. The bureau also reduced the number of scheduled examinations by approximately 50%, shifting its attention toward depository institutions , activities it deemed actual consumer fraud and areas within its statutory authority. Mortgage origination and servicing remain among its supervisory priorities. Under its new approach, the CFPB said examinations will focus on clearly identified products and potential violations tied to specific laws and regulations. The bureau also plans to avoid duplicating oversight already conducted by state or other federal regulators. Mortgage rules under review The CFPB is pursuing several mortgage-related regulatory changes under President Donald Trump’s executive order on promoting access to mortgage credit. Among its priorities is a review of the ability-to-repay requirements and qualified mortgage definitions under Regulation Z. The bureau is evaluating whether to modify the requirements, which apply to most residential mortgages. The CFPB is also considering a final rule to streamline mortgage servicing requirements under Regulation X. The proposal, initially issued in July 2024, is intended to simplify the loss-mitigation review process and make it easier for servicers to assist borrowers who experience payment difficulties. In July 2026, after the report’s primary reporting period, the bureau also issued a request for information seeking feedback on ways to promote access to mortgage credit. The CFPB additionally finalized changes to its fair lending and small-business lending rules. In April, the bureau amended Regulation B, which implements the Equal Credit Opportunity Act. The rule removed longstanding language supporting disparate-impact liability and revised restrictions on discouraging prospective credit applicants. It also prohibited for-profit creditors from using race, color, national origin or sex as eligibility criteria for Special Purpose Credit Programs . A separate May rule revised requirements for small-business lending data collection under Section 1071 of the Dodd-Frank Act. Among other changes, it lowered the annual revenue threshold for businesses covered by the rule from $5 million to $1 million, removed certain data collection requirements and extended the compliance date to Jan. 1, 2028. Fair lending and enforcement The bureau said it did not cite any fair lending violations during the reporting period, and that while it continued investigations, it instead focused its efforts on cases involving intentional discrimination with identifiable victims. It also made no referrals to the Department of Justice for potential patterns or practices of lending discrimination. Overall, the CFPB said it closed approximately 40% of its pending investigations as part of its effort to align enforcement with its revised priorities. The bureau reported receiving approximately 8.27 million consumer complaints between July 1, 2025, and June 30, 2026. It sent approximately 7.5 million complaints to companies for review, and companies responded to 99.6% of those complaints. The report's complaint figures come as the CFPB has moved to limit the public availability of consumer complaints. In August, the bureau said it would stop publishing unverified complaint narratives and related data visualizations in its public database, arguing that the accounts present only one side of a dispute and may not reflect violations of law. The bureau also said it would continue collecting complaints, reviewing company responses and sharing information with regulators. Previously published narratives will remain available through its Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) reading room.
