items.title: Higher Rates, Economic Uncertainty Push Banks To Tighten CRE Lending Standards
items.description: Banks tightened lending standards for commercial real estate loans in the third quarter as they placed more scrutiny on borrowers amid continued economic uncertainty. Unsplash/Markus Winkler The Federal Reserve ’s Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey on Bank Lending Practices, released this week, showed that banks are raising the bar on CRE lending for all loan categories, including construction, land development and multifamily. Demand for CRE loans weakened over the same period, according to the survey . The survey pulled responses from 61 domestic lenders and 18 U.S. branches of foreign banks. It also found that commercial and industrial lending standards were tightened for small firms but not large or middle-market firms. The 10-year Treasury yield surged past 5% last month amid rising debt concerns, hitting its highest level since 2002 before falling to 4.8% . Commercial lenders are now adopting a higher-for-longer interest rate policy as inflation and the war in Iran drag on the U.S. economy, Commercial Observer reported earlier this week. Many landlords are bracing for a wall of loan maturities coming due this and next year at interest rates much higher than they were several years ago, adding pain to borrowing costs. Private equity has stepped in to offer lending, but the Fed survey found that banks have also tightened lending to nondepository financial institutions, including business and mortgage credit intermediaries and private equity funds. Banks said NDFIs saw an increase in demand for loans, especially from small business and private equity funds, due primarily to working capital, liquidity needs and increased refinancing needs. items.title: Jemal Equities Buys Carr Properties' Former HQ In Receivership Sale
items.description: One of the most active office buyers in D.C. has purchased yet another property in the center of the city. Jemal Equities, founded last year by Matthew Jemal , the son of Douglas Development head Douglas Jemal, paid $45M for the office building at 1615 L St. NW, D.C. deed records show. Google Maps The 417K SF office building at 1615 L St. NW in downtown Washington, D.C. The 417K SF property, which sits a block away from the Farragut North Metro station, was previously owned by Carr Properties but has been controlled by a receiver since 2024. A judge with the D.C. Superior Court approved the sale by the receiver in July, court records show. Two limited liability companies managed by Jemal, 1615 L FS LLC and Jemal's RI 1615 LLC, took out a $48M loan for the purchase from NEG Financing I LLC, deed records show, $45M of which was used for the acquisition. Jemal Equities and Carr Properties didn’t respond to requests for comment. The office building at 1615 L was 27.6% leased as of September, according to special servicer commentary filed in Morningstar Credit’ s database, down from 67.6% occupancy as of the end of 2024. The building lost a two-floor tenant in January 2025, a full-floor tenant that April, and another full-floor tenant that August, according to the servicer commentary. 1615 L was built in 1984 and renovated in 2018. Carr purchased it in 2016 for $229M , assuming a two-piece $134M CMBS loan. It housed Carr’s headquarters there until Carr moved into its Midtown Center development down the street this year. Carr failed to pay off its CMBS debt at maturity in September 2023, and a court appointed a receiver, Trigild, in July 2024. The property’s valuation has dipped drastically over the past 13 years. At the time of its securitization in 2013, 1615 L was appraised at $213M. But that number dropped to $51M as of last October, according to Morningstar Credit’s database. Trigild selected Cushman & Wakefield to lease the office space in July 2025, court documents show. At the time, the brokerage said it had 300K SF available , more than 200K SF of which was contiguous. Over the last year , Jemal Equities has purchased at least four other office buildings in D.C. proper. Last month, it paid $92.3M for a BXP office building on Connecticut Avenue anchored by Steptoe. That came after its May purchase of a Navy Yard office building for $93M. The firm this week launched its website, which lists not just office but also retail, hotel and multifamily holdings. Conversely, Carr has been quickly shedding office assets in the city over the past 18 months while shifting to focus on multifamily development . In mid-2025, it handed over three of its D.C. assets to a J.P. Morgan Asset Management fund as part of an equity buyout, Bisnow first reported at the time. Around the same time, it sold at least two other D.C.-area office buildings: 4500 East-West Highway in Bethesda and 901 K St. NW in the District. items.title: Secure borders. A stronger economy. Washington must deliver both
items.description: In the first 100 days of the Trump administration, business leaders at residential construction and development companies were, in effect, summoned to the nation's capital for an all-hands meeting with administration officials on housing affordability. The summons came on short notice, on a Sunday afternoon. The invitation carried an undertone. Attend or else. The Washington, D.C., meeting never took place. But the episode captured the breakneck pace and take-no-prisoners approach of those early, flood-the-zone months. It also dialed in a distinctly unsettling tone for the rules of engagement between the new administration and the nation's private-sector business leaders in one of the economy's critical engines: homebuilding. Now, following the 2026 midterm elections, those rules of engagement stand an opportunity to change. Business leaders, including corporate strategists and their representatives on Capitol Hill, have a window to act quickly, elevate their priorities, and press for policy changes that have damaged or threaten to undermine some of the nation's most important economic capabilities. For homebuilding, residential development, and residential investment, immigration enforcement belongs near the top of the agenda. The United States needs secure borders and enforceable immigration laws. It also needs the workforce capacity to build homes, grow food, manufacture products, and sustain economic growth. These are not competing national interests, and treating them as such has real economic consequences. The question for President Trump, the incoming Congress, and the business leaders with a stake in the outcome is whether the next two years can achieve a more rational, workable balance among those objectives. For the housing industry, evidence of what's at risk is already accumulating. When enforcement collides with production Over recent months, HousingWire TBD has documented the increasingly disruptive effects of immigration enforcement on residential construction businesses and their trade partners. Builders and contractors report job site interruptions, workers reluctant to report for work, and crews disappearing from construction schedules. In some affected markets, executives have reported reductions of 60% to 80% in available trade crews. These are accounts from specific businesses and markets, not nationwide estimates. The disruption also extends beyond workers who lack legal authorization. Reports that U.S. citizens and legally authorized workers are apprehensive about reporting to job sites suggest that enforcement-related fear can diminish workforce availability and productivity. Residential construction depends on the coordinated sequencing of specialized trades. When a framing crew is unavailable, subsequent work may be delayed, schedules are extended, financing costs accumulate, and closings slip. For builders and their trade partners operating with already compressed margins and limited capital flexibility, repeated disruptions can pose a serious business risk. These accounts do not establish that immigration enforcement has caused a nationwide construction crisis. They do, however, raise a question policymakers cannot responsibly ignore: Are enforcement practices achieving legitimate security objectives while imposing avoidable economic costs on lawful workers, responsible employers, and American households? The workforce evidence is unmistakable A study published on October 8 by Harvard University's Joint Center for Housing Studies found that foreign-born workers accounted for 35% of the nation's construction trades workforce in 2024, compared with 18% of the overall U.S. labor force. Their representation is especially high in trades critical to home completion: 57% of drywall and ceiling-tile installers, 53% of roofers and painters, and 51% of flooring installers were foreign-born. Harvard's research found that foreign-born workers accounted for all net growth in the construction trades workforce from 2013 to 2024. Separate NAHB research found that Hispanic workers represented 32.8% of the construction workforce in 2024, up from 23.6% in 2010. In Texas and California, approximately six in 10 construction workers are Hispanic. Foreign-born status, Hispanic ethnicity, citizenship, and legal employment authorization are distinct characteristics. These statistics cannot be used interchangeably to describe immigration status. Nor do they, nor can they, truly reflect the full impact of foreign-born workers on job site capability and productivity because many undocumented frontline crew members are not counted at all. The statistics, however, illustrate the industry's substantial dependence on a diverse workforce, whose lawful participation must be protected. Meanwhile, labor shortages are worsening despite reduced housing production. NAHB's September 2026 survey found that, averaged across nine consistently tracked trades, 47% of builders reported labor shortages, up from 42% in April 2025. Framing shortages reached 57%, while finished carpentry shortages reached 58%. NAHB also identified immigration-enforcement-related worker apprehensions as a contributor to worsening shortages, along with competition from other construction sectors. Immigration enforcement did not create the industry's longstanding workforce problems. Those problems reflect decades of insufficient domestic workforce development, shifting demographics, competition for skilled labor, and limited productivity gains. But making an already constrained workforce even less available cannot be a rational part of a national housing affordability strategy. A workable policy foundation is already in place Washington does not need to start from scratch. Bipartisan immigration reform initiatives have repeatedly recognized the need to combine effective border security, lawful employment pathways, immigration-system modernization, and solutions for established workers and employers. items.title: NYC pied-a-terre tax notices get an appeals court green light
items.description: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's administration won another round on the pied-à-terre tax Wednesday, when a state appeals court dismissed a homeowners' lawsuit that had upended the surcharge's rollout. Appeals judges threw out an earlier Staten Island judge's ruling ordering the city to cancel about 17,000 notices. They found the homeowners lacked standing and weren't injured by the notices. All four judges agreed. The surcharge is a pillar in the city's plan to close a $12 billion budget gap. State officials projected it would raise about $500 million a year. The comptroller estimates the impact at closer to $1 billion before exemptions and appeals. Wednesday's decision does not directly affect a separate suit by billionaire casino magnate Steve Wynn, former Trump administration Commerce Secretary Wilbur Ross and his wife. They have challenged the state law behind the tax. That case remains pending in Suffolk County, with hearings scheduled in December. A Staten Island judge had ruled Sept. 29 that the city skipped individualized decisions before mailing notices. The judge called the notices arbitrary and capricious and a due process violation. Under the order, the Department of Finance was to cancel the notices and pull its roll from the agency website. New notices were allowed after an individualized review. Within hours, the city appealed and invoked a stay, so implementation continued. Little impact on luxury home market Residential brokers told HousingWire TBD that the legal back-and-forth and the tax itself have had little impact on the owner-occupied market. Ian Slater, co-founder and CEO of Trove Partners , said the market for under $5 million slowed in September and October. "We hit a record number of contract signatures above $5 million in September and October," he said. Wealth from a soaring stock market, plus nerves about its froth, is pushing buyers into top-end property, Slater said. Those buyers are "fully ignoring the pied-à-terre tax." Some want second homes in New York City, he said. However, listings of such properties remain scarce. Jessica Chestler, co-founder of The Chestler Jacobs Team at Douglas Elliman , said bidding wars have erupted. Supply isn't keeping pace with buyer demand, including for homes priced above $5 million. "We recently represented a buyer in a bidding war that we ultimately won, but it required going $1 million over asking on an apartment that needed a complete gut renovation," Chestler said. Why the panel reversed Because the homeowners lacked standing, the court never ruled on whether the NYC Department of Finance's rollout was lawful. The court said other arguments were either without merit or unnecessary to resolve. Finance later used 2025 tax data to revise its determinations, the court noted. Several hundred owners learned they did not owe the surcharge. The surcharge covers only non-primary residences. Through July 2028, the measure impacts houses worth $5 million or more. Co-ops and condos face a $1 million threshold. Wynn and the Rosses sued in late September. They argue the surcharge is an illegal property tax that discriminates against nonresidents. Wynn's notice totaled $183,094.69, while the Rosses' notice came to $83,531.52. Trove Partners' Slater does not expect the climate to change. "Political winds are clearly against the wealthy class," he said. He doubts judges or politicians will move away from the tax. "It's definitely an annoyance, but it's a bit of much ado about nothing," he said. Related More: New York City Property Tax

items.title: Court Calif. new-build buyers: Prop 37 funds up to 17% down
items.description: Court Calif. new-build buyers: Prop 37 funds up to 17% down By Andrew Martinez CloseText About Andrew twitter andrewomartinez mailto andrew.martinez@arizent.com linkedin andrewomartinez Published November 04, 2026, 4:26 p.m. EST 3 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Key Insight: Learn how California's newly passed Proposition 37 changes down payment obligations for buyers eying new construction. Supporting Data: A study suggests the measure could support 190,000 new home purchases statewide. Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. Processing Content California voters may have delivered a reprieve to local real estate players dealing with weak housing demand. Golden State residents Tuesday passed Proposition 37 by a comfortable margin , agreeing to kick off a unique revenue bond that will help homebuyers cover down payments for new builds. The $25 billion bond could support 190,000 new home purchases statewide, according to one analysis. The ballot measure, spearheaded by a Democrat statehouse veteran, passed alongside the blue wave nationwide as voters reacted to factors including rising costs. Californians also passed Prop 1 on Tuesday, which will allow the state to sell $11.25 billion in bonds to fund various affordable housing programs. Prop 37, or the California Middle-Class Homeownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026, will offer eligible home buyers up to 17% of a newly constructed home's purchase price for homes priced below $1.5 million. Borrowers eligible for the second mortgage must be California residents, occupy the home, and earn less than twice of their area's median income. Homeowners also must put at least 3% down on their purchase. An analysis noted another affordability perk as those consumers wouldn't also have to obtain mortgage insurance . The California Association of Realtors, which backed the proposition, didn't respond to a request for comment Wednesday. Mortgage players, including locally-based lenders and trade groups, didn't weigh in on the measure before Tuesday's election. Although California is one of the nation's most expensive states to buy a home, the proposition could nudge buyers stalled in some of the worst housing market conditions this decade. It can also provide slight relief to homebuilders which have seen demand for home loans on new construction fall notably this summer . How the proposition can boost homebuying An analysis by a consulting firm described the typical savings, such as a homebuyer securing a $27,044 down payment versus a $180,290 on the median-priced California home of approximately $901,450. The study, also citing Zillow and U.S. Census Bureau data suggests that every $1 billion of bond capital could support the construction and purchase of around 7,600 new homes across 21 California metropolitan areas. Additionally, every $1 billion of bond investment could leverage an additional $4.9 billion in spending on construction and related activities. Former Speaker of the California Assembly Robert M. Hertzberg championed the proposition in a recent op-ed , citing the state's massive housing affordability challenges. "Proposition 37 offers middle-class Californians a real chance to put down roots, build equity, and stay in the communities they serve," he wrote. Where the opportunity lies in California According to public statistics from the California Department of Housing and Community Development, the biggest homebuilding opportunity lies in Southern California. Of the 40,309 single-family properties permitted last year, 1,636 were in Los Angeles while 1,294 were in Los Angeles County. Builders however are completing more builds across the state. Of the 34,523 homes completed in 2025 per the database, a leading 1,248 properties were finished in Bakersfield last year. That was followed by Roseville and Elk Grove, outside of Sacramento, and Los Angeles. Andrew Martinez Reporter Andrew Martinez joined National Mortgage News in January 2022. items.title: Revere, MA Weighs 1,700-Unit Housing Project
items.description: Revere, MA Weighs 1,700-Unit Housing Project The city of Revere is eying a large redevelopment plan that would create 1,700 new affordable and market-rate homes about five miles northeast of downtown Boston. The Revere Housing Authority presented a proposal to the Revere City Council last week requesting a zoning change that would allow for development on a 40-acre site at Cooledge Street, near the city’s main street and commercial district, as reported this week by the Revere Journal . The phased development plan would create about 790 new public housing units, replacing the existing 431 units on the site, while adding roughly 910 market-rate units as well as community amenities and public open spaces. Out of the public housing units, 570 would be family units while 220 units would be designated for senior and the disabled. Current residents of the existing housing units, which are about 70 years old, would be relocated on-site while construction is ongoing being moved into the new units. RHA’s plan would create Revere’s third Smart Growth district, leveraging a planning tool established by the state’s Smart Growth Zoning and Housing Projection Act that is intended to promote affordability and mixed-use development. items.title: NAR: Repeat buyers dominate home sales as first-time buyers struggle to enter the market
items.description: NAR: Repeat buyers dominate home sales as first-time buyers struggle to enter the market by Jacqui Mueller November 05, 2026 Repeat buyers accounted for 78% of home purchases in 2026, while first-time buyers made up just 22%, showing the gap between repeat buyers and those buying their first home, according to the National Association of REALTORS® ' 2026 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers . The share of first-time buyers rose slightly from 21% in last year's report, which was a record low, but remains well below the historical norm of 40% before 2008. Their median age remained 40, the highest on record. Repeat buyers had a median age of 62, tying the previous record. That gap was also clear in how buyers paid for their homes. Thirty percent of repeat buyers purchased with cash, while their median down payment was 19%. First-time buyers made a median down payment of 9%, and 10% purchased with cash, the highest share recorded for that group. Among first-time buyers who paid all cash, 28% used an inheritance. That compares with 9% of first-time buyers who financed their purchases. The median age of first-time all-cash buyers was 54, compared with 38 for those who financed. Repeat buyers also had a median household income of $127,000, up from $111,700 in the previous report. Fifty-seven percent used proceeds from the sale of their previous home for a down payment. First-time buyers relied most heavily on personal savings, with 62% using that source. Thirty percent used financial assets such as retirement accounts, stocks or cryptocurrency, while 25% used gifts or loans from family and friends. Ten percent used an inheritance for a down payment, the highest share recorded. Financial assets have now accounted for a larger share of first-time buyer down payment sources than gifts or loans for two consecutive years. Saving for a down payment remained a major obstacle. Twenty-eight percent of first-time buyers identified it as the most difficult step in the buying process, compared with 6% of repeat buyers. Among buyers who had difficulty saving, 50% cited high rent or an existing mortgage payment. Credit card debt was cited by 35%, student loans by 32% and car loans by 31%. The financial sacrifices made to buy a home also differed between the two groups. Sixty-two percent of first-time buyers said they made sacrifices to save for a down payment, compared with 31% of repeat buyers. Buyers said they cut back on nonessential purchases, entertainment and clothing, and some canceled vacation plans. The report also found that 29% of first-time buyers carried student loan debt, compared with 10% of repeat buyers. The median student loan debt among buyers with those loans was $35,000. How buyers are approaching homeownership The profile of buyers is changing in other ways, too. Four percent of buyers purchased with unromantic roommates, an all-time high. Among first-time buyers, that share was 5%. Fourteen percent bought multigenerational homes, often to care for aging parents (30%) or save money (23%). The desire to own a home remained the leading reason for first-time buyers (60%) to make a purchase. Among repeat buyers, 18% said they wanted to be closer to family and friends, while 13% wanted a larger home. Finding the right property remained a challenge for buyers. Fifty-six percent identified it as the most difficult step in the homebuying process. For first-time buyers (39%), understanding the steps involved in purchasing a home was the biggest challenge. Buyers spent a median of 10 weeks searching for a home. Forty-six percent began the process by looking online for properties, while 19% contacted a real estate agent first. Overall, 53% found the home they purchased on the internet, 28% through an agent and 8% through a friend, relative or neighbor. The role of real estate agents Despite the challenges facing buyers, real estate professionals continued to play a central role in transactions. Ninety percent of buyers used an agent or broker, the highest share recorded. That figure rose to 93% among buyers of previously owned homes. Finding the right home was the service buyers most wanted from their agents (51%). Another 15% prioritized help negotiating the terms of a sale, while 12% wanted help with price negotiations. Agents also helped buyers navigate the process and evaluate properties. Fifty-five percent said their agent pointed out features or faults they had not noticed, and 54% said their agent helped them understand the homebuying process. This was especially important for first-time buyers, with 78% saying their agent helped them understand the process, compared with 47% of repeat buyers. Most buyers still found their agent through personal connections. Forty percent found their agent through a friend, neighbor or relative, while 23% worked with an agent they had previously used. Among first-time buyers, 52% found their agent through a personal referral. Just 1% of buyers found their agent through an AI search. Sellers also continued to rely on real estate professionals. Ninety-two percent used an agent or broker, a record high, while for-sale-by-owner transactions accounted for 5% of sales, matching the all-time low. Homeowners stayed in their properties for a median of 12 years before selling, the longest period recorded in the report. That was twice the six-year median recorded between 2000 and 2008. Moving closer to friends and family was the leading reason for selling, cited by 22% of sellers. When choosing a listing agent, sellers (31%) placed the greatest importance on the agent's reputation. Another 24% identified honesty and trustworthiness as the most important factor. Sellers most often wanted help marketing their homes and setting a competitive price (20%). items.title: Democrats Eye Tougher Data Center Regulations as They Regain Control of Congress
items.description: Democrats who rode data center discontent to victory in the midterms are expected to pursue strict new regulations on data centers when they take control of Congress in January. The Democratic sweep flipped dozens of House and Senate seats, and a number of those races hinged on broadsides against Republicans for their purported support of the industry. Meanwhile, voters considered more than 40 local measures to constrain data center development, and almost all of them passed. The results are likely to bring new life into Democrats' efforts to add guardrails to the artificial intelligence buildout. But their majority does not go far enough to override a veto from President Donald Trump , who has sought to aggressively promote data centers in the United States, in the pursuit of what he dubs "super intelligence." Polls show broad concerns that the pace of data center construction could drive up power costs , raise land prices, and create environmental problems. Recent Realtor.com® research on data centers found they're increasingly moving into rural areas. "If the Democrats take control of Congress, it could be a major problem for data center developers," Balaji Tammabattula , CEO of BaRupOn LLC, which develops energy infrastructure for data center companies, recently told Realtor.com. Data center companies, he said, are already reconsidering future investments. In Texas , Senate winner James Talarico released a blueprint for data center regulation with more enforcement. The state has a temporary moratorium on data centers in place, which Democratic Gov.-Elect Gina Hinojosa has pledged to extend. Just a few hours before polls closed, The Hill reported that Microsoft, Amazon, Meta, Google, and other tech companies were considering a more formal framework for data center development. "Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Elon Musk posted on X shortly after the results came in. What's on the table Congress' one effort to rein in the impacts of data centers fell short just before the midterms. Several weeks ago, the House passed a bill to encourage utilities to shield ratepayers from the costs associated with data center buildouts, the Ratepayer Protection Act . That followed widespread backlash against data center buildouts . But Senate Democrats tanked the bill because it didn't go far enough. They've coalesced around a few competing ideas for how to regulate data centers at the federal level. In the meantime, Democrats put forth their own bill, the Guaranteeing Rate Insulation from Data Centers (GRID) Act , with more enforcement power and penalties. Among its powers, it would require data center developers to provide their own energy, so they don't pull from the local power grid. It would also require more disclosure about data center developments and give the government the power to issue fines. Also, 20 Democrats signed on to a bill that would create a total moratorium on data center development. But the president has veto power, and he has opposed such a harsh move. Trump has advocated for data center development in the United States to prevent the technology being developed abroad. In the face of public backlash, he convened technology leaders in Washington in September and asked them to self-police the build-out of super intelligence. The White House also released an accord signed by those major companies committing to developing the technology safely. Trump called it "morally binding." Loading... Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei leaves the U.S. Capitol surrounded by aides and security after meeting with President Donald Trump on Sept. 29. Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images What it means locally While data centers affect property taxes , the exact impact on homeowners' tax burden is complicated. And the study found no impact on property values from large facilities in the two years after they open. Democrats may find an opening to create more rules around data center construction. Although Democrats also took control of governor's offices in many major states with data center developments, Realtor.com senior economist Jake Krimmel says that doesn't necessarily mean they will lead to sharp constraints on data centers. "Utilities costs, rather than home values, are probably the biggest immediate change voters are feeling or fearing," Krimmel says. "Our analysis of data center impacts on the housing market found essentially no effect on inventory or sales behavior so far." The Urban Institute suggested a few levers to help data centers support housing affordability. It suggested tax relief or energy cost offsets for communities that host many data centers. Otherwise, they risk straining local housing markets due to rising electricity costs, especially in high-growth regions. Meanwhile, Brookings suggested an electricity tax on data centers or some kind of offset to local governments. But it warned that regulation of the sector could encourage developers to build more centers overseas. It's unlikely the currently divided Congress will use the remainder of its term to pass rules around data centers. But when the new one comes in, it can reintroduce the GRID Act or other bills. The GRID Act’s 20-megawatt threshold would cover essentially the entire pipeline, more than 99% of planned capacity, Krimmel says. "That would give homeowners the most direct protection on rates," Krimmel explains. "Requiring new projects to bring their own power could also slow data center development, and the jury is also still out on the local economic and labor market impacts of data centers on localities." items.title: Mortgage Rates Fall for Third Straight Week After Democrats’ Midterm Triumph
items.description: Mortgage rates retreated to a new one-month low as bond yields softened in the wake of the historic midterm elections in which Democrats reclaimed control of the House and Senate. The average rate on 30-year fixed home loans drifted to 7.18% for the week ending Nov. 5, down 6 basis points from 7.24% the prior week, according to Freddie Mac . For perspective, rates averaged 6.22% one year ago. "Mortgage rates continued their downward trajectory this week, improving the environment for prospective homebuyers against a backdrop of strong economic growth," says Sam Khater , Freddie Mac's chief economist. The downward drift of mortgage rates is partly the byproduct of markets digesting the seismic shift of power in Washington, DC, and looking ahead to Friday’s October jobs report, according to Realtor.com® senior economist Hannah Jones . Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey released Tuesday came in stronger than expected, with layoffs down slightly and a significant gain in job openings. That points to a potentially solid monthly employment data. For homebuyers, however, a robust expansion of payrolls could be a double-edged sword. "While solid hiring supports housing demand over time, a stronger-than-expected report could also lift bond yields and slow the pace of rate declines in the near term," warns Jones. A strong labor market will also give the Federal Reserve cover to raise its benchmark rate further, a move the central bank is expected to make next month. Mortgage rates closely track 10-year Treasury yields. When Treasury prices fall, yields rise, pushing mortgage rates higher, and the reverse is true when bond prices pick up. Tuesday’s election results suggest Democrats successfully tapped into voter dissatisfaction with the economy under President Donald Trump , helping Democrats flip multiple traditionally red states blue. Yet, Jones says that it is too early to tell whether the shift will be reflected in the housing market. "Many newly elected representatives have voiced discontent with the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, which has contributed to rising inflation, so any progress toward resolution could mean lower inflation and softer mortgage rates ahead," she notes. Loading... Although rates have eased over the last three weeks, they remain above 7%, keeping many buyers on the sidelines. October marked another month of a slowing housing market , with both buyers and sellers pulling back. Pending sales fell 10.5% year over year, the steepest decline in three years, as buyers contend with diminished purchasing power. New listings fell 7.5% year over year as sellers held back, discouraged by weak demand. Still, sellers aren’t delisting in droves , which suggests they are merely hitting the pause button rather than acting out of distress. "With 43% of active listings having had a price reduction, buyers who can afford to participate are in a relatively strong position, facing less competition and more price cuts," concludes Jones. How your credit score affects your mortgage Your credit score plays a role when you apply for a mortgage . A credit score will determine whether you qualify for a mortgage and the interest rate you'll receive. The higher the credit score, the lower the interest rate you'll qualify for. The credit score you need will vary depending on the type of loan. A score of 620 is a "fair" rating. However, people applying for a Federal Housing Administration loan might be able to get approved with a credit score of 500, which is considered a low score. Homebuyers with credit scores of 740 or higher are typically considered to be in very good standing and can usually qualify for better rates, which can reduce monthly payments. Snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in New York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.

items.title: Absolute Home Mortgage, First Option leaders on strengthening their partnership
items.description: On Wednesday, Absolute Home Mortgage Corp. and First Option Mortgage announced a strategic transaction that combines the companies' resources and aims for originations growth amid a consolidating market . Matthew VanFossen , the CEO of New Jersey-based Absolute, and Alvin Shah, managing partner at Georgia-based First Option, sat down with HousingWire shortly after the announcement to offer further details. The deal, which combines the two companies with Mortgage Equity Partners — a wholly owned subsidiary of Absolute — is positioned to originate about $4 billion annually across roughly 420 producing loan officers. The leadership team will also expand as Shah and Kurt Nikolai, president and managing partner at First Option, join Absolute's ownership group and board of directors. Editor's note: This interview has been edited for length and clarity. Neil Pierson: This transaction is not considered to be a merger or acquisition. How would you describe it? Matthew VanFossen: It's lane three. Alvin and I, when we do business together, we never go down the two traditional paths. You could do mergers, you could do you asset sales, or we could have a buy-in situation. Usually it's one company taking over another, but this is First Option, the business partner, buying a piece of Absolute Home Mortgage in an equity deal . Maybe the headline should have been First Option acquires part of Absolute Home Mortgage, because that's what's going on. Absolute is the surviving entity in the transaction, but First Option's brand will be alive. Their entire team will be onboarded. Alvin and Kurt are joining the board of directors and have an ownership share in the entity — of course, pending regulatory approval. Alvin Shah: Obviously there's a much bigger picture in mind. For me personally, we were looking for an exit strategy for my partner Kurt over the next several years anyways, so that was top and center in terms of what was going through my head. But the opportunity to work with the Absolute team, it's not something new. I mean, we're already partners in a technology company, Mortgage Automation Technologies . Pierson: What is some of the history behind your partnership? Shah: Matt started the BIG Point of Sale several years ago, and because of the Lenders One network, I was exposed to it. And when we saw what he was building, it was great. It's a point-of-sale system built by lenders for lenders, so we jumped on board right away. We made an investment into the company. It kind of forced Matt's hand, allowing me to be on the board of directors over there as well. So we've all been working together for three, four years now. When everything transpired with First Option and what we were looking for long term, and also knowing what Matt was building long term in terms of the previous acquisitions he was involved in, the fit made sense right right away. I wanted growth, he wanted growth, and we knew what kind of damage we can do when we work together. The question was, will the cultures within the organizations match? Unbelievably, it was such a great fit where the leadership at First Option and the leadership at Absolute, we almost immediately became just like family. Now, it doesn't hurt that we've been friends and partners for so long, so a lot of the things that we did from a process standpoint, and from a vendor and technology standpoint, were already in line for both companies. So change from that standpoint was minimal. Pierson: Can you provide more perspective on what appears to be the start of more deals to come? What do you look at when thinking about growing through M&A or equity partnerships? VanFossen: Typically, for the the past four transactions we've done, I led up the M&A efforts. I would do the due diligence on the relationship management, the financials , but it's not my strongest suit. I might have been a little lucky. My strong suit is looking at technology and vision for the future — what we should be bringing in-house, what we should be developing. We have strategic partnerships on the board of directors that we have to be looking at. We're doing business with multiple mortgage companies. I quickly learned that Alvin was better a better deal-maker than I am. He was better at sorting out the strategic numbers, the fits, the technology alignment. Part of these past three or four years, we got our companies 90% in line with the same vendors , just from saying, "Hey, these vendors work." items.title: Longbridge profits drop even as Ellington's earnings indicate resilience to higher rates
items.description: Ellington Financial reported net income of $40.4 million in the third quarter of 2026, down from $54.4 million in the second quarter , as lower earnings from its reverse mortgage subsidiary Longbridge Financial , weighed on results. The Old Greenwich, Connecticut-based mortgage real estate investment trust reported earnings of 31 cents per common share for the quarter ending Sept. 30, compared with 43 cents per share in the second quarter. Adjusted distributable earnings, a non-GAAP measure, totaled $58 million, or 45 cents per share, down from $74.6 million, or 59 cents per share, in the second quarter. The company said adjusted distributable earnings exceeded its quarterly dividends. Book value per common share was $13.53 as of Sept. 30, compared with $13.61 at the end of June. Despite the lower earnings performance, Ellington president and CEO Laurence Penn said the company delivered strong results in the face of rising interest rates and widening yield spreads late in the quarter. "We generated GAAP net income of $0.31 per share and an annualized economic return of 9.4%, preserved book value per share, and produced adjusted distributable earnings in excess of our dividends," Penn said in a statement. "Looking ahead, our diversified business model and proprietary sourcing channels, together with our flexible balance sheet and disciplined risk management, should position us well to capitalize on the attractive investment opportunities that we see developing in the wake of the recent spikes in interest rates and volatility.” The company investment portfolio segment generated $61.1 million in net income attributable to common stockholders, down from $74.2 million in the second quarter. Ellington said its investment portfolio benefited from retained tranches of non-QM and agency-eligible securitizations, commercial mortgage bridge loans and investments in loan originators, particularly LendSure Mortgage Corp. Strong credit performance across its loan businesses also contributed to results, with 90-day delinquency rates declining sequentially. The company's adjusted long investment portfolio increased 4.5% sequentially to $4.7 billion at the end of September. Growth was driven by purchases of residential transition loans , closed-end second lien loans, agency-eligible residential mortgages, prime jumbo loans and commercial mortgage bridge loans. The portfolio's net interest margin increased to 3.55%, up from 3.36% in the second quarter, as higher asset yields partially offset increased funding costs. Longbridge performance Longbridge reported $12.5 million in net income attributable to common stockholders, down from $30.2 million in the previous quarter. Adjusted distributable earnings fell to $8.6 million from $28.9 million. The decline primarily reflected narrower origination margins and lower gains from proprietary reverse mortgage securitizations, according to the company. During the company's earnings call, Penn said that interest rates kept Longbridge's margins compressed. "Although Longbridge's contribution to earnings declined from the prior quarter, that prior quarter was extraordinarily strong, with two proprietary reverse securitizations completed," he added. Longbridge originated $676.3 million in loans during the quarter, up 36% year over year and 15% from the second quarter. Originations included $258.5 million in Home Equity Conversion Mortgages (HECMs) and $417.8 million in proprietary reverse mortgages. The company's net Longbridge portfolio increased 59% sequentially to $1 billion as of Sept. 30. Much of that increase was reversed following the October settlement of a proprietary reverse mortgage securitization that was priced in September. "Despite higher rates, September was Longbridge's strongest month ever for proprietary reverse submissions," JR Herlihy, Ellington's chief financial officer, said during the call. Longbridge also reported a quarterly record for its share of the HECM Mortgage-Backed Securities ( HMBS ) market, reaching 31% and ranking as the market's second-largest issuer, according to Bloomberg data cited in Ellington's report. During the quarter, Ellington completed its acquisition of a controlling interest in Statebridge Company , a diversified loan servicer . Statebridge serviced approximately 14,700 loans with a combined unpaid principal balance of $1.9 billion as of Sept. 30 — nearly all for third-party clients. Penn said the acquisition is expected to help Ellington apply its data and workout expertise to delinquent loans and real estate-owned properties , with the goal of improving loss mitigation and recoveries. Ellington also issued $150 million in additional 7.375% senior unsecured notes due in 2030, bringing the total outstanding in the series to $550 million. The company said strong institutional demand helped it secure a yield spread approximately 70 basis points tighter than its previous issuance last year. The company had $269.5 million in cash and cash equivalents, along with $1.92 billion in total unencumbered assets, at the end of the third quarter. Ellington repurchased 329,045 common shares at an average price of $11.44 per share after the quarter ended. During the third quarter, it issued approximately 2.5 million shares through its at-the-market program at an average price of $13.61 per share. items.title: Revere Housing Authority Seeks Zoning Change For 1,700-Unit Redevelopment
items.description: A large-scale redevelopment of an aging public housing complex is moving forward in Revere. Google Maps Revere Housing Authority on Cooledge Street in Revere The Revere Housing Authority filed a proposal with the city to create the Cooledge Street Smart Growth Overlay District across a roughly 39-acre site, paving the way for a 1,700-unit project, according to a Sept. 30 memorandum from RHA . The housing authority presented the proposal to the Revere City Council last week, the Revere Journal first reported . The redevelopment would replace the 431 public housing units on the site with 790 new public housing units — plus 910 market-rate units. Of the new public housing units, 570 would be family units and 220 would be set aside for seniors and the disabled. The project would also have public open space and community amenities. The proposed district has Cooledge Street running through its center and is bounded by Cushman Avenue, Gordon Road, Proctor Avenue and Broadway. It is down the street from Revere's main business district on Broadway. Earlier this year, RHA completed its comprehensive master planning process, in which it identified a long-term vision for the community through a mixed-income neighborhood redevelopment. The redevelopment is planned to take place in phases over the next five to 25 years. The city established similar smart growth districts in other neighborhoods on Green Street and Shirley Avenue in 2023. These smart growth districts fall under the state's Chapter 40R program, which was enacted in 2004 to encourage housing production near transportation, commercial areas and existing infrastructure to promote affordability and mixed-use development. The overlay would allow property owners to either utilize the underlying zoning or the new smart growth zoning. RHA says the district could allow Revere to receive zoning incentives and density bonus payments. The housing agency hasn't said whether it will bring on a private developer to build the market-rate housing. Similar projects are underway in Boston, where the Boston Housing Authority has partnered with private developers to build mixed-income projects on public housing properties. WinnCos . in June 2025 broke ground on the first residential building as part of the $1B Mary Ellen McCormack housing redevelopment in Boston. In total, the development would replace all 1,016 public housing units and build an additional 2,284 rental units. In April, Leggat McCall landed a $122M loan for the second building in its $1.4B Bunker Hill Housing redevelopment . In total, the project will deliver close to 2,700 housing units, including the replacement of 1,010 deeply affordable housing units. items.title: Invesco Closes $97.6M DST Offering
items.description: Unsplash/micheile henderson Invesco Real Estate Income Trust’s IREX V Diversified Portfolio Delaware statutory trust offering is fully subscribed at $97.6M, the nonlisted REIT announced . The offering launched in April. IREX V features one mixed-use office and retail property and one industrial property in North Carolina and South Carolina. The assets span roughly 353K SF and are 98.7% occupied. They were sourced by Invesco REIT. “As more property owners look to step away from the day-to-day demands of active management without giving up their real estate exposure, we continue to see strong interest in solutions that pair the tax-deferral potential of a 1031 exchange with professionally managed, diversified portfolios,” Invesco Real Estate Director, Private Markets and 1031 Exchange Program Kyle Connor said in a press release. It isn’t just Invesco seeing the strong interest in DSTs. Sales of the investment type totaled nearly $8.4B through October, a 26% increase from the less than $6.7B raised through the same period in 2025, according to data from Mountain Dell Consulting . In October alone, DST sales totaled roughly $918.5M, an approximately 9.6% increase from September’s $838.3M. Industrial and multifamily are the most widely offered asset types, representing 34% and 31% of all syndicated offerings, AltsWire reported. Big-name institutional investors including Ares , Hines and Blackstone are creating DSTs , a more than 20-year-old investment vehicle that has gained popularity this year as older investors seek passive investment opportunities. The investment vehicle is a securitized form of a 1031 exchange , which allows property owners to avoid paying taxes when selling an asset if they invest their gains in another deal within a certain time frame. DSTs allow individuals to own fractional interests in commercial real estate assets while remaining hands-off, as fund managers take care of the assets. items.title: Fannie, Freddie Complete Fraud Reviews On Walker & Dunlop
items.description: Walker & Dunlop is ready to move on from the investigations brought by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac that led to repurchasing fraudulent loans and significant quarterly losses over the last year. Google Maps Walker & Dunlop's headquarters at 7272 Wisconsin Ave. in Bethesda, Maryland The Maryland-based company announced in its third-quarter earnings call Thursday that Fannie and Freddie conducted and concluded their investigations and it doesn’t expect further loan buybacks or losses, CEO Willy Walker said on the call . "After months of investigations and loan-level analysis across our portfolio, it is extremely reassuring to know that both investigations are complete, yet we are still managing the real estate and notes that we repurchased over the past two years," Walker said. "Those assets have required significant ongoing investment and quarterly marks that were going to impact Walker & Dunlop’s earnings potential for many quarters to come." W&D's total revenue fell 12% year-over-year to $298.4M, and debt volumes declined 5%, according to a release on the company's third-quarter results. The decrease is in line with the 11% decline in transaction volume, primarily due to a higher portion of brokered transactions at a lower fee. Shares were down less than a percentage point to $38.28 on Thursday morning, but they are down nearly 35% year to date. W&D originates loans and sells them to Freddie and Fannie. It is so active in the space that it has become the largest Fannie multifamily lender . In December 2025, Freddie asked the commercial real estate finance and advisory services firm to investigate $100M across two loan portfolios because of fraudulent documentation submitted by the borrower, The Real Deal reported . W&D's internal investigation found that three portfolios totaling roughly $134M in Freddie Mac loans were impacted by fraud. The findings led to the company recording a $29M loss expense and firing members of its banking staff in February after finding they didn’t adhere to its loan origination process and failed to detect fraudulent behavior. Originators are typically responsible for covering legal costs and repurchasing the loans when fraud is detected. W&D negotiated an agreement with Freddie Mac over a $50.7M portfolio, delaying its repurchase through the end of 2027. The remaining two portfolios totaling $83.6M were still under negotiation. It is unclear where negotiations stand now. In the second quarter, W&D reported $23.2M of operating and credit-related charges tied to defaults on loans it repurchased and an agreement to cover a greater share of losses on nearly $16M in defaulted Fannie Mae loans, according to a release.
